newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MAJOR COMPANIES CHEER AFRICAN OIL PROSPECTS.
newsitem.headline: MAJOR COMPANIES CHEER AFRICAN OIL PROSPECTS.

text.p: Foreign companies are poised to pour money into Africa's rich oil and gas deposits, providing partnerships can be forged with national oil companies (NOCs) within investor-friendly environments.

"We're going to invest several billion dollars in Africa over the next few years. Our production is growing in Africa. Africa is becoming increasingly important," John Cousins, Mobil Oil Corp Europe and Africa vice president told Reuters.

While praising Africa's discovered and vast untapped oil and gas reserves, major oil exploration and development companies -- represented at the Africa Upstream 1996 conference -- also preached collaboration with NOCs.

"We're a global business and major companies go where the business environment is most favourable. Countries, companies and NOCs have to work together to come out with value at the end of the day," Cousins said on Friday.
Companies also emphasised the importance of speedily applying advanced geological and drilling technology to bring as yet unexploited reserves to fruition.

Focusing on the deep water of Africa's west coast, Janet Stoner, exploration and production vice president for Texaco, said that Texaco was successfully applying to those waters advanced technology proven in the Gulf of Mexico.
British Petroleum was also looking at the west coast:
"The possibility that we have in mind is that future production opportunities lie off Africa in the deeper water," David Bamford, head of BP's sub-Saharan Business Unit said.
Deep water zones were those lying between 200 metres and 2,000 metres and were provinces which contained billions of barrels of oil and several giant fields.
Delegates also urged governments to provide stable economic and political environments to investors which would guaranteed adequate earnings for risky investments.
South African Minister of Mineral and Energy Affairs Penuell Maduna, in his opening address on Wednesday, hit the nail on the head cautioning African states:
"Oil and gas explorers are not here to primarily provide energy to Africa. They are here to economically exploit oil and gas. In short they are here to make profit," he said.
But foreign companies remained deafening in their applause for Africa's wealth of energy reserves, saying that international exploration focus was now on the continent.

Shell International exploration and production vice president Erik van Scherpenzeel said that in-house estimates by Shell indicated that about 50 billion barrels of oil and 350 TCF of gas could still be discovered in Africa.
"These are signifcant figures," he said on Friday.
The conference saw the launch and inaugural meeting of the African Institute of Petroleum (AIP), whose membership base includes representatives from companies, governments and NOCs.

"The aim of AIP is to facilitate collaboration and partnerships, to create a sharing of synergies between major companies and NOCs. Good business is good for all parties," said AIP president Samuel Dossou-Aworet, who is also chairman of Petrolin UK, an advisor to Gabon on petroleum affairs.
